column2: Then the revered Karttikeya, filled with great wrath, split Mount Krauncha, which echoed with the cries of krauncha birds, with the spear given by Fire.
With its sala trees and straight trunks, its monkeys and elephants terrified, its shore-birds frightened, serpents falling out,
resounding with fleeing hosts of langurs and bears, with the noise of deer running and sumaras bewildered and thronging,
with sharabhas and lions suddenly bounding out, that mountain, though fallen into a pitiable plight, yet shone.
The Vidyadharas who dwelt on its peaks flew up, and the Kinnaras were alarmed, startled by the sound of the spear's fall.
Then Daityas rushed forth by hundreds and thousands from that blazing best of mountains, wearing wondrous ornaments and garlands.
The Kumara's attendants overtook and slew them in the fight, and Fire's son, slayer of heroes, split Krauncha with the spear.
Making itself manifold and single by the great soul's power, the spear hurled in battle came back again and again to his hand.
Such was the power of the revered son of Fire; by him Krauncha was split and Daityas slain by hundreds.
Then the revered god, having slain the foes of the gods, honoured by the gods, attained supreme joy.
Then, O king, drums resounded and conches, Bharata, and the divine women showered unsurpassed rains of flowers.
The holy wind blew, bearing divine fragrance, and Gandharvas and sacrificing great sages praised him.
Some affirm him to be the lord, the Grandsire's son, Sanatkumara, the eldest of all, the womb-born of Brahma.
Some say he is the son of Maheshvara, some the son of Fire, some of Uma, of the Krittikas and of the Ganga.
Single, twofold and fourfold, the mighty god, lord of yogins, in hundreds and thousands.
This I have told you, O king, the consecration of Karttikeya; hear also the holiness of the Sarasvati's line of tirthas.
When the foes of the gods were slain by the Kumara, great king, it became the best of tirthas, like a second heaven.
Staying there, the lord, Fire's son, then gave sovereignties separately in the three worlds to the chief Rakshasas.
Thus at that tirtha the revered one, destroyer of the Daitya race, was consecrated, great king, by the gods as general of the gods.
That tirtha is named Aujasa, where in former times Varuna, lord of the waters, was consecrated by the hosts of gods, bull of the Bharatas.
Bathing at that best of tirthas and worshipping Skanda, the plough-bearer gave Brahmanas gold, garments and ornaments.
Spending the night there, Madhava, slayer of heroes, honoured that best of tirthas and touched its water; the plough-bearer, best of Madhavas, became glad and pleased at heart.
All this has been told to you, as you asked me, how the revered Skanda was consecrated by the assembled gods.

Hearing which I know myself purified, ascetic; my hair stands on end and my mind is serene.
mahabharata:9:46.3	Having heard of the Kumara's consecration and the slaying of the Daityas, I have supreme joy and yet more curiosity.
mahabharata:9:46.4	How was the lord of the waters consecrated here by the gods and asuras? Tell me that, greatly wise one, for you are skilled, best of men.
[Vaishampayana said:] "Hear, O king, this wonder of the former kalpa as it was. At the beginning, in the Krita age, as it proceeded in due order, all the gods, assembling, said this to Varuna:
'As Shakra, king of the gods, ever protects us from fears, so do you too become lord of all rivers.
And your dwelling shall be always in the sea of the gods, the abode of crocodiles; this ocean, the lord of rivers, shall be under your sway.
With Soma you shall have waning and waxing.' 'So be it,' said Varuna to those gods.
Then all assembled and made Varuna, dweller in the ocean, lord of the waters, by the rite seen in the scriptures.
Having consecrated Varuna, lord of aquatic creatures, the gods honoured the lord of waters and went to their own places.
Consecrated by the gods, the greatly renowned Varuna also guarded rivers, oceans, streams and lakes duly, as Shatakratu guards the gods.
Then, touching the water there and giving wealth of many kinds, the greatly wise slayer of Pralamba went to Agnitirtha, where Fire, lost, was not seen in the womb of the shami tree.
When the destruction of the worlds seemed to appear, blameless one, they approached the great-souled Grandsire of all the worlds.
'The revered Fire has vanished and we do not know the cause; let not all the worlds perish; let him restore Fire to us.'
[Janamejaya said:] "Why did the revered Fire, sustainer of the worlds, vanish, and how was he found by the gods? Tell me that truly."
[Vaishampayana said:] "Greatly afraid of Bhrigu's curse, mighty Jatavedas (Fire) entered the womb of the shami tree and vanished.
When Fire had vanished, all the gods with Vasava, greatly distressed, searched for the lost blazing one.
Then, reaching Agnitirtha, they saw Fire there dwelling duly in the womb of the shami tree.
All the gods, tiger among men, led by Brihaspati, reaching that Fire, were pleased; they went as they had come, and he became the devourer of all.
By Bhrigu's curse, O king, as the expounder of Brahma had said, bathing there too, the wise one went to Brahmayoni.
Where the revered Grandsire of all worlds created—bathing there, Brahma with the gods of old created foods for the deities duly.
Bathing there and giving wealth of many kinds, he went to Kubera's tirtha, where, practising great austerity, the lord Ailabila (Kubera) obtained lordship of wealth, O king.
Dwelling there, O king, wealth and treasures attended him; the plough-bearer then went to that tirtha, and bathing duly gave wealth to Brahmanas.
He saw there that place in Kubera's excellent forest, where of old the great-souled one practised vast austerity,
where King Kubera obtained abundant boons: lordship of wealth, and friendship with Rudra of immeasurable splendour,
godhood, guardianship of a quarter, and a son, Nalakubara, which the lord of wealth readily obtained, mighty-armed one.
He was consecrated there too, meeting the hosts of Maruts, and a swan-yoked, lovely vehicle was given him there, the divine Pushpaka aerial car, and lordship over the Rakshasas.
Bathing there, O king, Bala gave abundant gifts and Rama, anointed in white, quickly went on to a tirtha,
frequented by all beings, named Badarapachana, with forests of every season, ever with flowers and fruit, auspicious.

There was a daughter of Bharadvaja, unequalled on earth in beauty, named Shruchavati, lord, a maiden, a celibate student.
mahabharata:9:47.3	She practised very severe austerity, O king, with many restraints, resolving, 'May the king of the gods be my husband.'
mahabharata:9:47.4	Many years passed for her, bull of the Kuru line, as she kept those severe and very hard observances for women.
mahabharata:9:47.5	Pleased by her conduct and austerity and devotion, O lord of men, the revered Pakashasana (Indra) was greatly pleased.
mahabharata:9:47.6	The lord, ruler of the gods, came to her hermitage, taking the form of the great Brahmin-sage Vasishtha.
mahabharata:9:47.7	Seeing that Vasishtha, best of ascetics, of fierce austerity, she honoured him, Bharata, with the customs seen by the sages.
mahabharata:9:47.8	Knowing the observances, the auspicious, sweet-speaking one said, 'Revered one, tiger among sages, what do you command, lord?
mahabharata:9:47.9	Today I shall give you everything to the best of my ability, good vower, but I shall not give my hand, because of devotion to Shakra.
mahabharata:9:47.10	By vows, restraints and austerity, ascetic, Shakra, lord of the three worlds, is to be pleased by me.'
mahabharata:9:47.11	Thus addressed, the revered god, as if smiling, looked at her and spoke, as if soothing her who knew the observances, Bharata:
mahabharata:9:47.12	'You practise fierce austerity; I know you, good vower; I know the purpose of this undertaking of yours, auspicious one, that is in your heart.
mahabharata:9:47.13	All that will come to be as it is, fair-faced one; everything is gained by austerity, everything rests on austerity.
mahabharata:9:47.14	Those divine stations of the gods, fair one, are to be won by austerity; austerity is the root of great happiness.
mahabharata:9:47.15	Having done fierce austerity here and laid down the body, men attain godhood, auspicious one; hear this word of mine.
mahabharata:9:47.16	Cook these jujube fruits, fortunate one, of good vows.' Having said Cook," the revered slayer of Bala departed.
Having taken leave of the auspicious one, he then recited a prayer, not far from that hermitage, at the excellent tirtha, Indratirtha, great king, renowned in the three worlds.
To test her, the revered Pakashasana, lord of the gods, made the cooking of the jujubes difficult.
Then, O king, restrained, silent and free of weariness, intent and pure, wrapped in a cloth, the strict-vowed one set them on the fire and cooked the jujubes, tiger among kings.
As she cooked, a very long time passed, bull among men, and they were not cooked, and the day waned.
The pile of wood she had was burned up by the fire; seeing the fire without fuel, she burned her own body.
First, the lovely one thrust her feet into the fire, and when they were burned, the blameless one thrust them in again and again.
Though her feet were burning, the blameless, lotus-eyed one did not mind the pain, desiring to please the great sage.
Then, seeing her deed, the lord of the three worlds was pleased and showed the maiden his own form.
The best of gods said to that maiden of firm vows: 'I am pleased with you, auspicious one, by your devotion, austerity and restraint.
Therefore whatever desire you wish shall be fulfilled for you, auspicious one; leaving your body, great lady, you shall dwell with me in heaven.
And this best of tirthas of yours, fair-browed one, shall be firm in the world, destroyer of all sin, named Badarapachana, renowned in the three worlds, bathed in by Brahmin-sages.
At this auspicious best of tirthas, great lady, the seven sages once left Arundhati and went to the Himalaya.
Then those greatly fortunate and strict ones, having gone there, went, it is said, to gather fruits and roots for their livelihood.
As they dwelt in the Himalayan forest seeking sustenance, a drought of twelve years came upon them.
Making a hermitage there, those ascetics lived; Arundhati too, the auspicious, was then ever devoted to austerity.
Seeing Arundhati keeping severe observance, the three-eyed one (Shiva), well pleased, came then as a boon-giver.
Taking a Brahmin form, the greatly renowned Mahadeva approached her and said, "Fair one, I desire alms."
The lovely woman replied to that Brahmana, "My store of food is exhausted, Brahmana; eat jujubes here." Then Mahadeva said, "Cook these, good vower."
So told, the renowned woman cooked them, out of desire to please the Brahmana, setting the jujubes on the kindled fire.
She heard then divine, charming, holy stories; that dreadful twelve-year drought passed.
While she fasted, cooked and heard the auspicious tales, that very dreadful time was for her like a single day.
Then those sages came back, bringing fruit from the mountain; and the revered one, pleased, said then to Arundhati:
Go to these sages as before, knower of dharma; I am pleased with you, by your austerity and restraint.
Then the revered Hara showed his true form, and then told them of her great conduct:

The austerity you have gained on the Himalayan back, Brahmanas, I do not think equal to hers.
mahabharata:9:47.42	By this ascetic woman very hard austerity was practised; fasting and cooking, twelve years were completed.
Then the revered one again said to Arundhati: "Choose a boon, auspicious one, whatever is desired in your heart."

The broad, copper-eyed woman said to the god in the assembly of the seven sages: "Revered one, if you are pleased with me, let this be an excellent tirtha, beloved of the perfected and divine sages, named Badarapachana.
Lord of the lords of the gods, whoever stays three nights here, pure, would gain by fasting the fruit of twelve years." Saying "So be it," Hara went to heaven.
The sages were astonished, seeing Arundhati unwearied and unchanged in colour, the chaste one enduring hunger and thirst.
Thus the highest success was attained by the pure Arundhati, as by you, great lady, of keen vows, for my sake.
Auspicious one, a special devotion has been offered by you in this vow, and so I give you something today, well pleased by your restraint.
I give you a special boon, fair one, in addition to the boon given to Arundhati by the great soul.
By his grace and your splendour, auspicious one, I shall declare another boon here, duly.
Whoever, composed, stays one night at this tirtha, bathing, will gain worlds hard to obtain after laying down the body.'
Having said this, the revered god, the thousand-eyed, the mighty, went again to heaven from the holy Shruchavati.
When the wielder of the thunderbolt had gone, O king, a rain of flowers fell there, bull of the Bharatas, divine and divinely fragrant.
Drums also resounded on every side with great noise, and the wind blew skilfully, bearing holy fragrance, lord of men.
Casting off her fair body, she became Indra's wife; having gained him by fierce austerity, she delighted with him, O Achyuta.
[Janamejaya said:] "Who was her mother, revered one, and where was that fair woman raised? I wish to hear, Brahmana; my curiosity is very great."
[Vaishampayana said:] "Seeing the Apsara Ghritachi, broad-eyed, approaching, the seed of the great Brahmin-sage Bharadvaja fell.
That best of those who recite prayers took up the seed in his hand and placed it in a leaf-cup; there that fair one was born.
Having performed all the birth-rites for her, the ascetic, the great sage Bharadvaja, gave her a name,
Shruchavati, the righteous one, in the assembly of the host of sages; and leaving her in the hermitage he went to the Himalayan forest.
Touching the water there too, the great one gave wealth to the great Brahmanas, and then the foremost of the Vrishnis, composed, went to the tirtha of Shakra.
There the king of the immortals performed a hundred sacrifices and gave Brihaspati vast wealth.
He performed there all the sacrifices as prescribed by the Vedic scholars, without restriction, with sacrificial animals and with various fees.
Those sacrifices, bull of the Bharatas, the greatly radiant one completed duly a hundred times, whence he is famed as Shatakratu.
From his name that tirtha is auspicious, holy and eternal, famed as Indratirtha, the liberator from all sins.
Touching the water there too, the pestle-armed one, duly, and honouring Brahmanas with drink, clothing and food, went from that auspicious tirtha to Ramatirtha,
where the greatly fortunate Rama, the Bhargava, great ascetic, repeatedly left the whole earth bereft of her bull-like kshatriyas.
Putting the sage Kashyapa, best of sages, in front as his teacher, he conquered by the Vajapeya and a hundred horse sacrifices, and gave the earth with her oceans as sacrificial fee.
Rama, having given wealth there to the Brahmanas, Janamejaya, and having touched the water as is right and honoured the twice-born,
at that holy tirtha in an auspicious place, giving wealth, the fair-faced one, and saluting the sages, came to the tirtha of the Yamuna,
where the greatly fortunate son of Aditi, Varuna, bright-lustred, performed the Rajasuya, O lord of the earth.
Having conquered men and gods in battle there, Varuna, slayer of heroes, performed the excellent sacrifice.
When that excellent sacrifice had been completed, a battle broke out between gods and Danavas, bringing destruction to the three worlds.
When the Rajasuya, best of sacrifices, was over, Janamejaya, a most dreadful battle arose against kshatriyas.
Then Rama, the plough-wielder, at that best of tirthas, bathing there and giving wealth to the Brahmanas, Madhava,
the wearer of the forest garland, glad and praised by the twice-born, from there the lotus-eyed one went to Adityatirtha,
where, having sacrificed, the revered luminary, the Sun, O best of kings, gained lordship over the luminaries and power.
On the bank of that river all the gods with Vasava, the Vishvedevas with the Maruts, the Gandharvas and Apsarases,
Dvaipayana, Shuka, Krishna Madhusudana, Yakshas, Rakshasas and Pishachas, lord of men,
these and many other thousands of yoga-perfected ones were at that auspicious, holy tirtha of the Sarasvati, scorcher of foes.
There in former times Vishnu, having slain the asuras Madhu and Kaitabha, bathed, bull of the Bharatas, at that best and excellent tirtha.
And the righteous Dvaipayana, bathing there, Bharata, attained supreme yoga and the highest perfection.
Asita Devala too, the great ascetic, in that very place, resorting to supreme yoga, the sage gained yoga.
Ever devoted to dharma, pure, self-controlled, laying down the rod, a great ascetic, equal toward all creatures in deed, mind and speech,
free of anger, great king, regarding praise and blame, pleasant and unpleasant as equal, seeing gold and a clod alike, the great ascetic,
ever worshipping the gods and guests together with the Brahmanas, delighted in celibacy, ever devoted to dharma.
Then, great king, the mendicant Jaigishavya, the wise sage, came there, resorting to yoga, composed at that tirtha.
That greatly radiant one lived in Devala's hermitage, O king, ever devoted to yoga, a great ascetic who had attained perfection.
While Jaigishavya the great sage lived there, Devala, while showing himself to him, did not by dharma engage him.
Thus, great king, a long time passed for the two, and Devala did not see the sage Jaigishavya.
At mealtime the wise wanderer, Janamejaya, knowing dharma, came to Devala at the time for alms.
Seeing the great sage arrived there in the form of a mendicant, he showed him supreme respect and great affection.
Devala honoured him to the best of his ability, Bharata, with the rite seen by the sages, composed, for many years.
Once, O king, a very great thought arose in the great-souled Devala on seeing the greatly radiant sage:
Many years have passed while I have been honouring him, and this lazy mendicant has said nothing to me.
Thus considering, the glorious Devala, travelling through the sky, took a pitcher and went to the great ocean.
As he went, the righteous one, to the ocean, lord of rivers, he saw Jaigishavya already gone there before, Bharata.
Then, astonished, the lord Asita fell into thought: "How has this mendicant reached the ocean and bathed there?"
Thus the great sage Asita thought; then, bathing duly in the ocean, pure, he recited his prayer.
Having finished his daily recitation, the glorious one went to his hermitage, Janamejaya, taking the pitcher filled with water.
Then, entering his own hermitage, the sage saw Jaigishavya sitting there in the hermitage.
Jaigishavya said nothing to him whatever; like a block of wood, the great ascetic dwelt in the hermitage.
Seeing him bathed in the ocean's water, like the ocean, he saw that he had also entered the hermitage before.
Asita Devala, O king, the wise one, thought of the power of Jaigishavya's austerity, born of yoga.
The best of sages thought, O king of kings: "I saw him in the ocean and in the hermitage; how is this?"
Thus considering, that sage, master of mantras, flew up from the hermitage into the sky, O lord of men, to test the mendicant Jaigishavya.
He saw there perfected ones moving in the sky, composed, and saw Jaigishavya honoured by those perfected ones.
Then Asita, deeply stirred, resolute, firm in vow, Devala, saw Jaigishavya going to heaven.
From there he saw him going to the world of the ancestors, and from the world of the ancestors he saw him going to the world of Yama.
Rising from there too, he followed the great sage Jaigishavya going to the praised world of Soma.
He rose to the auspicious worlds of those who sacrifice single-mindedly, then to the worlds of agnihotris, and from those he rose too.
From those ascetics who perform the new-moon and full-moon sacrifices, the wise one saw him go to the worlds of animal-sacrificers; he saw a stainless world worshipped by the gods.
To the abode of those ascetics who sacrifice with the various Chaturmasya rites, and to that of the Agnishtoma sacrificers, he saw him go.
To the abode obtained by those ascetics who sacrifice with the Agnishtuta, Devala saw him follow.
He saw him in the worlds of the greatly wise who perform the best of sacrifices, the Vajapeya, and those with much gold.
Devala saw Jaigishavya in the worlds of those who sacrifice with the Pundarika and the Rajasuya.
He saw him in the worlds of the best of men who perform the Ashvamedha, the best of sacrifices, and likewise the Naramedha.
Devala saw Jaigishavya in the worlds of those who perform the hard-to-obtain Sarvamedha and the Sautramani.
Devala saw Jaigishavya in the worlds of those who sacrifice, O king, with the twelve-day and various other sessions.
Then Asita saw him gained to the worlds of Mitra and Varuna and likewise of the Adityas, attaining union with them.
In a moment the strong one slew all that stood in his sight, and with the limbs and bodies of them, lord of men, the whole circle of the banyan tree was covered on every side.
One not fighting dies, and one fighting lives; when Time arrives, great king, none gets past it.
Then my anger vanishes as I look at his feet; for my thought is that Karna's feet are like Kunti's.
[The hunter said:] "If I am held the cause truly, then another would be the contriver here, and a sinner in the destruction of a creature."
This man, appointed by the Lord, does good and bad deeds; what is there to lament in that?
Then that king, O great king, the leader of the Pandavas, slayer of heroes, honoured those words and did as they said.
And the constellations, struck again and again by the planets, were seen by all, but they did not see themselves in any way.
Then they went, along the northern shore of the salt sea, tiger among the Bharatas, to the south-west quarter.
Covered with austerity, dreadful, green with grass of hair, mixed with the odours of sinners, a mire of flesh and blood.
